newsitem.title: USA: Retail inventories jump in July.
newsitem.headline: Retail inventories jump in July.

text.p: Retail inventories jumped at the sharpest rate in 1-1/2 years during July, the Commerce Department said Monday, boosting stocks of unsold goods on the shelves of all types of businesses.

Total business inventories rose 0.4 percent in July to a seasonally adjusted $1 trillion after being revised to show no change in June. Previously, the department reported that June inventories had risen 0.1 percent.
Recent reports have shown some moderation in the pace of consumer spending at start of the second half, which analysts said likely played a role in the higher July inventories.
Retail inventories climbed 1.1 percent to $307.52 billion -- the biggest increase since a 1.3 percent surge in January 1995 -- after a slight 0.1 percent June increase.
Auto inventories, which show up in the retail figures, rose strongly by 1.4 percent to $86.1 billion, the largest addition to monthly supplies since a 2 percent jump in March 1995.

Automakers were expected to add to their supplies of new cars on dealer lots for fear of a strike this fall. Negotiations are currently under way between the Big Three domestic automakers and the United Auto Workers union.
There were only fractional increases in wholesale and manufacturing inventories in July.

Economist Cynthia Latta of DRI/McGraw Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass., noted that new-car sales were relatively weak in July before rebounding in August and said that was a factor in backing up retail inventories.

"But I don't think it suggests any developing inventory glut because the other components of the inventories report are right in line with expectations," she said, adding that consumer spending probably will be less buoyant in the third quarter but was unlikely to drop sharply.

Last Friday, the Commerce Department said August retail sales edged up only 0.2 percent after a 0.1 percent gain in July. That helped fire a market rally by implying the economic expansion was cooling from its second-quarter pace so that Federal Reserve policy-makers might decide not to raise interest rates next week.
"I think we're going to see some fallout on consumer spending from the huge consumer debt load but it won't be a retrenchment, just a little more saving and a little less spending," Latta said.

During July, manufacturers' inventories grew by 0.2 percent to $434.52 billion after a 0.1 percent decline in June. Wholesalers' inventories were up 0.1 percent to $259.45 billion following a 0.2 percent June gain.
Total business sales in July grew by 1.2 percent to $720.55 billion after a 0.5 percent drop in June.
The inventory-to-sales ratio -- a measure of how long it would take to sell existing stocks at the current pace -- fell to 1.39 months' worth in July from 1.40 months in June.
